problem: Existing evaluations of VLMs on visually interactive decision-making (robotics, computer use, games) are domain-specific and observational, offering little systematic, controlled diagnosis of domain-agnostic factors such as history length, observation modality, feedback and goal visibility. Few frameworks combine diverse domains, scalable episodes, partial observability and SFT/RL training support.
motivation: VLMs do well on static vision-language benchmarks and text-based multi-step tasks, but it is unclear how they integrate visual observations into multi-step decisions. A customizable gym with controllable difficulty and oracle solvers allows cross-domain controlled experiments that isolate what limits interactive decision-making and what training data helps.
key_idea: VisGym is a Gymnasium-based suite of 17 customizable long-horizon visual interaction environments with function-call actions, textual feedback and oracle solvers, used to diagnose frontier VLMs through controlled ablations and to train them by SFT.
insight: Controlled ablations show that context helps only up to about 4 turns before full history hurts, that ASCII text observations raise GPT-5 by 3-4x on symbolic tasks (a perception bottleneck), and that removing textual feedback lowers performance for all models. Showing the goal image can backfire because perception errors make the model judge different images as identical (Gemini 2.5 Pro: 80% and 57% errors on Zoom-In and Matchstick Equation). In SFT, information-revealing demonstrations matter more than data quantity: Matchstick Rotation success rises from 32.9% to 70.0%, and continued training on baseline demos degrades Mental Rotation.
method: Function-conditioned action space: actions are function calls with parameters (e.g. ('swap',(1,2))), using models' function-calling ability across domains
Function instructions: each task supplies a natural-language description of its functions and argument constraints in the initial prompt for zero-shot rollouts
Environment feedback: textual feedback per action (invalid format, out of bounds, executed) alongside the visual transition; a unified step function handles parsing, validation, execution and reward
Oracle multi-step solvers: heuristic solvers per task with multiple strategies (BFS/DFS, swap/reorder) and optional stochasticity for diverse SFT demonstrations
17 environments with difficulty parameters: real and synthetic, full and partial observability, known and unknown dynamics; easy and hard configurations (e.g. Maze 9x9 vs 11x11, Jigsaw 2x2 vs 3x3)
Diagnostic ablations: history truncation (1/2/4/inf turns), ASCII text observations, removal of textual feedback, goal image at start, plus StringSight failure-mode discovery
SFT protocol: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct fully finetuned on solver demos (easy only) in single-task and mixed-task settings; module-wise finetuning (vision vs LLM) and information-revealing data curation

setting.backbone: 12 VLMs evaluated zero-shot (Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Grok 4 Fast, Qwen-VL-Max, Qwen3-VL-235B, GLM-4.5V, Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Gemma 3-27B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B); finetuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
setting.training_data: Solver-generated demonstrations from easy-level episodes in the VisGym environments (single-task: 1,500 steps; mixed-task: 5,000 steps; batch size 64, lr 1e-5); trajectories that fail or overlap test states are filtered; source images from LLaVA, LVIS, RefCOCO, SS2, Objaverse
setting.observation: Rendered images (real or synthetic) at each step plus textual feedback and full or truncated interaction history; ASCII text variants for four tasks
setting.action_space: Function-call actions with parameters (e.g. swap, rotate, move, mark, stop), with a step limit of 20 (easy) or 30 (hard)
setting.simulator: Gymnasium-based VisGym (MuJoCo Fetch, custom mazes, puzzles)
setting.privileged: none (oracle solvers used only to generate SFT data; goal image given only in the goal-visibility ablation)

numbers_note: These figures are the paper's own benchmark, so they are not comparable to standard navigation benchmarks. Per-model and per-task results and the finetuned-model averages appear only in figures (not extracted). The paper reports no navigation benchmark numbers.
results: The best frontier model, Gemini-3-Pro, reaches only 46.61% (Easy) and 26.00% (Hard) average success across 17 tasks. SFT of a 7B model on solver demonstrations reaches state-of-the-art on most tasks (numbers in figures only). Qwen3-VL-8B generalizes to hard variants about 2x better than Qwen2.5-VL-7B (easy 0.59 vs 0.64).
limitations: Mostly synthetic and puzzle-style tasks; only two are robotics/navigation-like (Maze 3D, Fetch), so it is a weak proxy for real embodied navigation
Finetuning results are limited to SFT on 7B/8B models; RL is supported but not run
Many results appear only in figures, and the analysis and conjectures are mostly observational, with success measured by a binary stop reward
